pages.text: Nigeria is one of the most biodiverse countries in Africa. Within its borders live more than 900 species of birds, nearly 300 species of mammals, and thousands of species of insects, reptiles, and fish. From the mangrove swamps of the Niger Delta to the savannah grasslands of the north, Nigeria is home to an extraordinary range of wild animals.

image.note: Map of Nigeria's ecological zones: mangrove coast, rainforest belt, guinea savannah, sahel

pages.text: Many people do not associate Nigeria with wildlife. They think of cities, oil, and people, of which Nigeria has vast numbers. But beyond the cities, Nigeria contains habitats that support some of the most remarkable animals in the world. Some of these animals are found nowhere else on earth. Some are critically endangered. All of them are part of Nigeria's natural heritage.
This book introduces some of Nigeria's most significant wild animals: where they live, how they behave, and what threatens them. Understanding these animals is the first step toward protecting them.

Nigeria's ecological range explains its wealth of species. In a single day of travel from the coast to the far north, you would pass through mangrove swamp, freshwater swamp forest, lowland rainforest, derived savannah, guinea savannah, sudan savannah, and finally the dry sahel. Each zone has its own community of animals. Few countries on earth pack so many different worlds inside one border. That is why Nigeria matters so much to African conservation.

Nigeria's rainforest, concentrated in the south and south-east of the country, is one of the most species-rich habitats in Africa. It is dense, dark, and alive with sound: the calls of birds, the crash of primates moving through the canopy, the hum of insects.

image.note: Illustration of Nigerian rainforest interior: multiple layers of canopy, shafts of light, diverse wildlife

pages.text: The Nigeria-Cameroon chimpanzee is one of the most endangered subspecies of chimpanzee in the world. It lives in the forests of south-eastern Nigeria and western Cameroon. Its population has declined dramatically due to deforestation and hunting. Conservation programmes in Gashaka Gumti National Park in Taraba State are working to protect what remains of its habitat.

The forest elephant of West Africa is smaller than the more familiar savannah elephant. It lives in dense forest, where its smaller size and straighter tusks allow it to move between trees. Forest elephants are extremely shy. They are rarely seen by humans and leave almost no trace of their presence beyond the wide paths they carve through the undergrowth. Their numbers have fallen sharply across West Africa.

The Cross River gorilla is the rarest great ape in the world. Fewer than three hundred individuals survive, living in a small area straddling the border between Nigeria and Cameroon. The Cross River gorilla is so rarely seen that most of what we know about it has been gathered from camera traps, tracks, and the nests it builds in trees to sleep in. It is classified as critically endangered.

image.note: Illustration of a Cross River gorilla in forest habitat with inset showing range map

pages.text: The African forest buffalo, smaller and redder than its savannah cousin, moves through the forest in small herds. The drill, a large and strikingly coloured primate, lives in the forests of Cross River State and is among the most endangered primates in Africa. The red river hog, with its vivid orange fur and white facial markings, is one of the most beautiful animals in Nigeria's forests.

The drill deserves a closer look. This powerful, short-tailed primate, related to the mandrill, lives only in the forests of south-eastern Nigeria, western Cameroon, and Bioko Island. Adult males have glossy black faces and impressive builds. Drills live in groups that can join together into troops of more than a hundred. The Drill Ranch in Cross River State, run by conservationists since 1991, has bred hundreds of drills for eventual return to protected forest.

The African grey parrot, one of the most intelligent birds on earth, was once common across Nigeria's forests. Greys can mimic human speech with uncanny accuracy and solve puzzles that challenge young children. That intelligence has been their misfortune: trapped in enormous numbers for the international pet trade, they have vanished from most of their Nigerian range. International law now bans the wild trade, but enforcement remains weak, and recovery will take decades.

The African manatee is Nigeria's gentlest secret. This large, slow aquatic mammal grazes on plants in the rivers, lagoons, and creeks of the Niger Delta. Fishermen occasionally encounter one dozing below the surface. Manatees are protected by law but threatened by hunting, accidental capture in nets, and the degradation of the delta's waterways. Most Nigerians will never see one, and many have never heard of them, which is precisely the danger.
North of the forest belt, Nigeria's landscape opens into guinea savannah: grassland dotted with trees, home to a different set of animals adapted to open ground, seasonal rains, and dry-season heat.

The lion once roamed across much of Nigeria. Today, Nigeria's lion population is small and fragmented, concentrated in a few protected areas including Yankari National Park in Bauchi State and Kainji Lake National Park in Niger State. Nigeria's lions are part of the West African lion population, which is genetically distinct from East and Southern African lions and is critically endangered.

image.note: Illustration of a West African lion in savannah grass, body slightly leaner than East African subspecies

pages.text: Yankari National Park is Nigeria's most important wildlife reserve. It protects a large area of guinea savannah in north-eastern Nigeria and is home to elephants, hippos, baboons, waterbuck, warthogs, and many species of birds. The park is best known for its warm-water springs, called Wikki Warm Springs, which attract both wildlife and visitors throughout the year.

The hippopotamus lives in Nigeria's rivers and lakes, spending the day submerged to protect its sensitive skin from the sun and emerging at night to graze on land. Despite their appearance, hippos are extremely dangerous. They are responsible for more human deaths in Africa than any other large land animal. They can run faster than a person and are fiercely territorial in water.

The African elephant is the largest land animal in the world. In Nigeria, elephants move across national park boundaries and sometimes come into conflict with farming communities whose crops they destroy. Managing this conflict between people and elephants is one of the most difficult challenges in Nigerian conservation.

Nigeria has two crocodiles worth knowing. The Nile crocodile, large and formidable, inhabits rivers and lakes and demands respect and distance. The dwarf crocodile, by contrast, rarely exceeds a metre and a half, hunts at night in forest streams, and spends its days hidden in burrows. It is heavily hunted for meat and is now endangered. A country's wildlife is not only its lions and elephants. It is also its small, shy, disappearing specialists.

Nigeria has lost an enormous amount of its wildlife in the past century. Deforestation, hunting, and the expansion of farming and cities have reduced or destroyed habitats that once supported vast numbers of animals. Several species that were once common in Nigeria are now extinct within its borders. Others are on the edge.

The pangolin is one of the most trafficked animals in the world. All four African species of pangolin are found in Nigeria. They are hunted for their meat and for their scales, which are used in traditional medicine in parts of Asia. Despite international protection, the trade continues, and pangolin populations across West Africa are declining rapidly.

image.note: Illustration of a pangolin curled in defensive position, showing scale detail

pages.text: The African wild dog, one of the most efficient predators on the continent, is believed to be extinct in Nigeria. The cheetah, once present in the north of the country, is also gone. Several species of antelope that were once widespread have been reduced to small, isolated populations.

Nigeria has a network of national parks and nature reserves. Their effectiveness varies enormously. Some are well managed and genuinely protect the wildlife within them. Others exist mainly on paper, with little funding, inadequate staffing, and serious problems with poaching. Expanding the capacity of Nigeria's protected areas is the single most important thing that can be done to preserve the country's remaining wildlife.

Understanding wild animals, knowing their names, their habits, and their stories, is the beginning of caring about them. Nigeria's wild animals are part of its national identity and its natural wealth. They belong to every Nigerian child alive today, and it is those children who will decide, in the decades to come, whether they survive.

Behind every protected animal stands a protector. Nigeria's park rangers patrol on foot through difficult terrain, confronting armed poachers for modest pay. Conservation scientists track gorillas by their nests and dung. Community leaders negotiate agreements that keep forests standing. Organisations such as the Nigerian Conservation Foundation run education programmes reaching thousands of schoolchildren. Conservation is not an abstract idea. It is a daily effort by particular people, many of them young, most of them unsung.

A child in Abuja or Lagos can help from home. Never buy wild animals, their skins, or products made from them. Visit national parks and zoos that fund conservation, and take others with you. Read and share the stories of Nigerian wildlife. Join or start a nature club at school. The animals in this book cannot argue their own case. They need Nigerians who know their names, know their worth, and are willing to say so out loud.
